query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying the eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a trace amount of boron will promote the in-situ formation of nanoscale ductile films along the internal lamellar boundaries, thereby simultaneously enhancing strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that act as crack initiation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor addition of boron during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under conventional melting and casting conditions with the only modification being the boron microalloying. Post-solidification thermal treatments remain identical to the unmodified baseline. Room-temperature tensile testing is performed to evaluate mechanical performance.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregates during solidification to the colony boundaries to form thin, continuous, ductile boron-rich interfacial films.
generation.mechanism: The boron-induced interfacial films enhance cohesion between the lamellar phases, reduce stress concentration at internal boundaries, and retard microcrack propagation during tensile loading. This mechanism improves load transfer and mitigates crack nucleation, leading to simultaneous increases in strength and ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the boron-microalloyed alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in both ultimate tensile strength and elongation at fracture at room temperature.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that suffers from brittle interfacial behavior leading to low room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: The enhancement is expected only when the boron content is precisely controlled; excessive boron could lead to the formation of brittle boride phases, negating the benefits or even deteriorating mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how boron will exactly partition during solidification and whether minor deviations in processing could inadvertently form detrimental phases. Detailed control of boron concentration and processing parameters is critical, and the long-term stability of the ductile interfacial films needs further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with the controlled addition of boron and one unmodified control set, using identical melting, casting, and thermal treatment procedures. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM) to assess the presence and distribution of boron-induced interfacial films.
measurements: Microstructural analysis of colony boundaries for evidence of continuous, ductile boron-rich films
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-microalloyed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility, or if brittle boride phases are observed at the colony boundaries instead of the predicted ductile films, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
